Red hake (Urophycis chuss) is a commercially important gadoid species distributed along the northwestern Atlantic continental shelf from the Gulf of Maine to Cape Hatteras. This demersal fish undergoes a pronounced ontogenetic habitat shift, with pelagic larvae and early juveniles residing in the water column before settling to the seabed as benthic adolescents. Field surveys conducted by the Northeast Fisheries Science Center have documented that females attain puberty at a total length of approximately 26 cm [Lp = approximately 26 cm], a size typically reached within the second year of life. This length-based threshold marks the onset of vitellogenesis and the individual's transition into the reproductively active segment of the population. Mature individuals exhibit a highly iteroparous life history strategy, investing considerable energy into somatic growth even after the initiation of gametogenesis. The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 66 cm [Li = 66 cm], a figure derived from long-term trawl survey data encompassing several decades of sampling effort across the species' range. These dimensions position Urophycis chuss as a medium-bodied gadid relative to its congeners, with growth trajectories that decelerate markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity.

Reproductive output in Urophycis chuss has been inferred from fecundity relationships established for the closely related white hake (Urophycis tenuis). After applying a weight-based correction factor, available data indicate that a mature female of this species produces approximately 1.3 million eggs per spawning season, achieved through an estimated 6.5 spawning events per year [F_R_i = 6.5 spawning events per year] with each event yielding approximately 200,000 eggs [N_R_i = each event yielding approximately 200,000 eggs] when maintained under laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This exceptionally high fecundity is consistent with a batch-spawning strategy in which multiple clutches of pelagic eggs are released sequentially over an extended spawning season. The species does not exhibit a discrete, brief spawning window; instead, gravid individuals are encountered in the fishery from late spring through early autumn, suggesting a protracted period of reproductive activity that maximizes larval encounter rates with suitable planktonic prey fields. Extrapolations from this reproductive schedule imply that an individual female can release many millions of oocytes over the course of a single breeding season, a pattern typical of gadids that exhibit high fecundity combined with low parental investment and high larval mortality.

The pelagic eggs of Urophycis chuss are small and spherical, measuring approximately 0.76 mm in diameter, a dimension that is consistent among several members of the genus. From this egg diameter, the wet weight at birth has been calculated as approximately 0.00023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00023 grams], reflecting the minimal maternal resource investment allocated to each individual offspring. This minute hatchling mass places the species at the extreme low end of the size spectrum among Northwest Atlantic finfish larvae and necessitates a rapid onset of exogenous feeding to avoid starvation mortality during the critical first-feeding period. The yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion with a relatively large yolk reserve that supports the individual through the initial days of development before the mouth opens and the larva must begin capturing planktonic prey. Observations from rearing studies indicate that the transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrition occurs swiftly, with the first feeding event typically taking place within two to three days after eclosion at ambient shelf temperatures.

As Urophycis chuss progresses through the juvenile phase and toward adulthood, somatic growth leads to substantial increases in body mass. Using the length-weight relationship of W = 0.00407 * L^3.11, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum recorded length of 66 cm has been estimated at approximately 1,850 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,850 grams]. A female that has just attained the length at puberty of 26 cm, by contrast, carries a predicted wet weight of roughly 102 grams [Wwp = roughly 102 grams] according to the same allometric equation. The nearly twenty-fold difference between the mass at puberty and the asymptotic mass highlights the considerable scope for post-maturational growth in this species, a life-history trait that allows older, larger individuals to contribute disproportionately to population reproductive output through greater fecundity. This pattern contrasts with semelparous gadids, in which growth slows or ceases entirely after the first spawning event. In Urophycis chuss, the extended growth phase is accompanied by continued investment in both gonadal tissue and somatic maintenance throughout the adult lifespan.

The lifespan of Urophycis chuss under prevailing thermal conditions in the Gulf of Maine, where bottom temperatures average approximately 9 °C [T = 9 °C], has been estimated at around 4,380 days [am = around 4,380 days], which equates to roughly twelve years of potential longevity. This maximum age estimate is derived from annual otolith increment counts obtained from commercial fishery discards and research survey specimens, providing robust empirical support for a relatively extended lifespan among medium-bodied gadids. The population's generation time, calculated from a moderate age at first reproduction and a maximum longevity of approximately 4,380 days [am = approximately 4,380 days], buffers the population against short-term recruitment failures, though the species remains sensitive to prolonged periods of poor larval survival at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. Comparative analyses with other members of the family Phycidae indicate that Urophycis chuss occupies an intermediate position on the fast-slow continuum, with a lifespan that is shorter than that of some deepwater congeners but considerably longer than that of short-lived estuarine-associated species within the same trophic guild.
